Seven pairs of communication types

blocks.html: We communicate in different ways in different places. The lecture groups them into seven pairs.

blocks.html:
Pair First type Second type
Inner vs Outer Inner — thoughts, imagination and feelings inside you. Not spoken. This is your inner chatter (the talk in your head). Outer — what you show through speech or action.
Personal vs Social Personal — with yourself, family, friends and dear ones. Social — outside your personal space: community, society, people at work, the world.
Verbal vs Non-verbal Verbal — the spoken word. Non-verbal — gestures, body language, facial expressions and paralingual cues (tone, pitch, speed of voice).
Written vs Oral Written — documents, agreements, reports, emails, messages. Oral — spoken discussions and opinions.
Internal vs External Internal — inside the organisation: within a team or between teams. External — with clients, vendors and teams outside the organisation.
Vertical vs Horizontal Vertical — up and down the hierarchy, between managers and team members. Horizontal — between peers (people at the same level), in the same team or across teams.
Formal vs Informal Formal — has a fixed process. Meetings, reports, briefings, minutes of meetings, feedback, appraisals. Informal — casual talks and chats over tea, coffee or lunch.

blocks.html: Cultures differ in how much the context (the situation around the words) affects the meaning.

blocks.html: High-context cultures — for example China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam: - People rely a lot on non-verbal and subtle situational cues. - A person’s official status, place in society and reputation matter a lot. - What is not said can matter more than what is said.

Four points from the lecture slide

Type 1: Passive listening

blocks.html: Passive listening means listening without interrupting.

blocks.html:
1. Listen without interruption. Wait for the other person to finish. If you only stop interrupting, you are already a better listener.
  2. Listen to the whole person. Do not listen only to words. Notice their voice, tone and body language. A raised voice saying “My mother is ill” also tells you: I am in distress.
  3. Acknowledge with small signals. Make sounds like “hmm”, “oh”, “I see”. Use gestures like nodding. This shows you are there.
  4. When to use it: mostly when a person is very distressed (very upset or crying). They just want to pour their heart out. Interrupting them at that time is silly.

Five barriers

blocks.html: Psychological, Language, Cultural, Organisational, Physical.
blocks.text: Psychological, Language, Cultural, Organisational, Physical.

blocks.html: Psychological barriers — inner chatter, preconceived notions, cognitive bias, lack of interest/attention/focus (boredom), emotional state (fear, anxiety, anger), limiting beliefs. - About 70,000 thoughts a day; 80–90% are unproductive. - Fully involved → thoughts near zero. Be in the present. - Emotions cause distortion: what I mean ≠ what I say ≠ what you hear.

blocks.html: Cultural barriers — culture is passed down generations; globalisation brings cultural diversity at work. - Head nod: side to side can mean “no” in some places; in others, slow = “yes”, fast = “no”. - German style: direct, direct eye contact. Japanese and Indian styles: polite, indirect. - High-context (China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam): non-verbal and situational cues, status and reputation matter; what is not said matters. - Low-context (Europe, North America): meaning is in spoken and written words; say “no” directly; structured, literal messages. - Overcome: study other cultures, learn values, observe and accept, be open-minded, understand mannerisms.

Tips for effective communication

blocks.html:
• Detail is lost at each step: understand → describe → listen → act.
  • Assumptions (whose left? whose right?) cause errors.
  • Small details matter. Repetition, questions and hand gestures help.
  • Exact copy → more instructions. Creative ideas → fewer instructions.
  • ABCs: Accuracy, Brevity, Clarity.
  • Give size, distance, direction and scale (map: 1 cm = 1 km).

Listening

blocks.html:
• Listening = paying attention to what someone is really trying to tell you.
  • Reduce the noise in your head; see with your ears.
  • Passive listening: no interruption; listen to the whole person (voice, tone, body language); acknowledge (“hmm”, nodding); used when someone is very distressed.
  • Active listening: animation and acknowledgement; paraphrase; ask for clarification; ask questions; mirror emotions.
  • Listening to the Future: listen for what the speaker desires; help them move forward; help them build hope and dreams.
  • Four filters: dislike, cultural difference, bias, different opinion or values.
  • Self-rating: we say 9/10; loved ones say 3–4/10.
